utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Could we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I have heard, we have no witness today. We have to concentrate on other issues. This is already the second time that we don't have a witness. As it states in the United States, isn't it, we have a rule of three strikes out. I hope that we'll, in future, not face the same situation again and always a witness is ready and prepared. But how does the OTP want to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the radio tape that Your Honour asked be played. We would like to play that first. We also have a group of documents, I think about 22 additional documents we would like to offer into evidence some time today. And just to explain to Your Honour or just to alert Your Honours and the Defence, we're having a lot of problems this month with witnesses. Two of the witnesses we had hoped to call have indicated that they refuse to come. One we can just no longer contact. They don't answer the phone. The other has indicated medical problems and will not come. We are trying to get other witnesses to fill those holes. It's difficult because as we come towards the end of the case, we have fewer witnesses left to ask to change their schedule. Many of them cannot do that. Many of the remaining witnesses are experts whose reports are not completed or not disclosed yet. One of the things we are considering is because of these two witnesses dropping out, we are considering filling the hole left from the lack of their testimony with either calling a witness who had earlier been listed as 92 bis or a witness that we had earlier decided did not contribute enough to call to the case, but that witness had been here and we did not call earlier. We haven't made a decision or actually contacted those witnesses yet. And we would have to then be asking the Court also for permission to move a witness back from 92 bis to live, on the basis that the witness who was going to testify live -- testify live about those events is no longer coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the parties when there are such problems, to contact the Chamber directly that we can find a solution. As it was indicated earlier, we are aware that there are elections in the near future, but nevertheless, on a daily basis, we have indeed to find out if the interest of justice demands that we hear the one or other witness in the area. And the Judges are prepared; it's a question of finding out if the security situation so allows or not. And if or not it's appropriate to go there. Please let us know what is necessary. On the other hand, when we have once decided that certain evidence can be introduced via 92 bis, we shouldn't, just in order to fill gaps and to use time, come back to hear a witness viva voce. I don't think that makes much sense. But we have discussed this in concreto on the basis of a concrete witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would like to play the audiotape that had the 65 ter number 440 and I believe it has the S number of 91 [Realtime transcript read in error "92"]. And the transcripts, I believe, are already distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe it's 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 91, right. Because I could read on the transcript 92. 91, that's right. We have already 91A and 91B. It's in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's call it 91B-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have additional copies of the English translation if that's needed, and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I wonder, if it's possible to hear a video, and at the same time hear the translation? But let's try it. Do you have any experience with this as regards the speed of hearing such a tape? Therefore, my suggestion would be let's hear it step by step, for example, if I can see here, it starts with Simo Miskovic. Why shouldn't we hear the first portion, the original voice of Mr. Miskovic, and then later on just hear the English translation before us, and then it's, of course, the possibility for both the Defence and the accused himself to give the one or other hint if the one or other believes that the translation may be incorrect or misleading. But to give us an impression, we should start hearing the audiotape until the end of the speech of Mr. Miskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we stop here at the end of this page. Thank you. May we then hear the English translation of the first page from B/C/S please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [As read] When the first T84 tank entered the barracks compound, I remember the joy and delight on both sides. That's the course we had charted to prepare people for the defence, and that is how we generally prepared for the defence in this region. I would also like to emphasise something which is typical of Prijedor. We have not had a single paramilitary or sabotage action in this region, and still the job was done. Although those from Sanski Most, Novi, Bosanska Dubica, and Dvor na Uni and other places offered to help, I did not allow that. After the establishment of the -- that is to say, we established an HQ here and linked up the units with battalion commanders and all the rest, so we were prepared for a possible showdown in this region. You are well aware of the events that ensued. However, as the president of the party and the chairman of the Crisis Staff, at the moment, my plan was that the takeover should be done on a nonworking day, Saturday or Sunday, in order to avoid conflict and bloodshed in this region. However, some other unexpected events prevented this. The telex from Jerko Doko was captured which explicitly ordered attacks on barracks, military facilities, police, the confiscation of artillery pieces, et cetera. "Immediately now," it read. It was already the 29th. I was at the meeting at that moment with Mr. Cehajic and Mirza Mujadzic at the SUP, that is to say, the Prijedor MUP. As soon as I finished there, when I learned about the telex, I went up to the barracks where Kuruzovic, Mico Kovacevic, and Stakic, Simo Jankovic, Cadzo and others were. And from the military side, there were Arsic and Zeka and the deputy Evic. During the conversation which was then held, I remember well Colonel Arsic, who then encouraged us. We were dealing with something uncertain, and thought that everything was supposed to be done perfectly and function excellently, because we did not have any experience. As a warrior who had already gone through Slavonija, he encouraged us by saying that not everything was that bad and that we should not have any problems and had good prospects of succeeding, since all the tasks in the military and police sectors had been accomplished. He said that they were not going to be any problems. He suggested that the best thing would be to do that -- to do that on the following day, since it was a working day. I remember when he decidedly asked me: "Who would you seize power from Saturday or Sunday, Simo? These are not working days. There's no one to seize power from." I took it jokingly then, but later I fully realised that his remark was right to the point. Having analysed everything in detail, and after everyone had clarified their stands, we realise that we were prepared. Then I scheduled a meeting of the Crisis Staff for 2.00 a.m. and ordered Mr. Kuruzovic and Simo Drljaca to do the job with the army, as we had agreed at the said meeting, and that they were going to submit the report by 2.00 a.m. We acted in accordance with this agreement and in the meantime, when I went home, Arsic and Zeljaja called me, informing me that Mirza appeared and wanted to talk and that it would be good if we all met. Of course, I arrived immediately. Later, during the conversation with Mr. Mujadzic, we agreed to go out for dinner that night, and Mirza proposed that we go to the Luna restaurant in Gomjenica, and I responded that that was not okay since we were after all local public figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then hear the end of this clip of Mr. Miskovic in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please -- could you please stop the B/C/S version. Thank you. We were already with the first sentence of the reporter. Now, the English contribution of Mr. Miskovic, please, until the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] And that we should be seen together downtown. And so, I proposed another venue, Evropa, but Mirza was not in the mood to go to Evropa, and then I insisted that we go to the Novi Hotel, and so we went to the Novi Hotel. Since I had some business to finish at home, I went home. And later, we, of course, went -- I saw that the plan had been changed in the meantime, and that they were not at the Novi Hotel. They were in the Europe restaurant. We stayed in the Europe and had dinner until around 11.00 p.m., and since I owned a cafe in the Mrakovica cinema, in the vicinity, after the dinner and the conversation we had -- I went to the cafe, and while I was there, until 40 past midnight or quarter to 1.00 past midnight, about five or six people came to the door and checked whether I was inside. They were probably scanning the situation and checking if anything was going to happen that night. The citizens remember well the rumours saying that they were going to slay people any night. Chaos was being created, and people were panic-stricken. Since they saw that there were many customers in the bar, and that I was behaving normally, they thought it was just another false alarm. At 2.00 a.m., I attended the session of the Crisis Staff when the reports were submitted that it was -- and it was decided by the Crisis Staff that the takeover would commence at 4.00 a.m. And that's how it started. It all went smooth. However, my main concern, like everyone else's, was the fact that nothing had been reported from the MUP yet. All the more so, since there were mixed patrols down there, and armed men, professionals, if you will, and I was afraid shooting might start and someone might get injured or killed, God forbid. When I received information that no harm had been done, I felt relieved, like everyone else, and then everything continued the way it did. That was the most important part that has to be told. I've already mentioned in the introductory part that we had already established authority in the assembly, and all our representatives of the SDS were tasked to be at their offices at 6.00 a.m. There were only five or six people who were not allowed to enter the municipal building, while all the rest functioned normally. That was yet another proof that the middle letter D, democratic, in the name of our party really meant something. Our intention was to break the permanent blockade with regard to the division of power and eliminate the possibility of surprise and intentional creation of chaos in this region. We had made a promise that these people would not be fooled and outsmarted for a third time in a row in history, and that's how we proceeded the way we did. I have no more to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We already had the next sentence of the reporter. Could you please also read this sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Reporter: Dear listeners, this was Mr. Simo Drljaca who spoke in detail about the preparations and the seizure of power. I have to say right away that here...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Question for the OTP, regarding the burden of proof, what do you believe was it the voice of -- question is not of belief here, how can you prove that the voice we heard one of Mr. Miskovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The voice of Mr. Miskovic as we can see it on the English translation, or is it true that what the reporter now says that we heard Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think if Your Honour reads the rest of this paragraph it's obvious that was a slip of the tongue, because the next sentence is "I have here also Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Kuruzovic who are going to comment upon these events from the point of view of the police and the army." And then it goes on to say: "Since Mr. Drljaca, Simo Miskovic said that the Crisis Staff concluded that it had been done and acted accordingly," it again refers to Mr. Miskovic. But the statements of the speaker that we heard first clearly indicate that it's Mr. Miskovic. First, Mr. Mujadzic testified that, in fact, he indeed did have dinner with Mr. Miskovic. Further, the speaker identifies himself as the president of the SDS party. We know from the documents presented that that was Simo Miskovic. He also identifies himself as the president of the Crisis Staff at that time. And the evidence that has been presented so far and will be perhaps even clarified further later is that the Crisis Staff was first set up an intraparty Crisis Staff was set up on the orders of the republic level, and that would have as the president, the president of the party, Mr. Miskovic. After the takeover, the Crisis Staff head was the president of the party, after it took on the prerogatives of a government. So I think the context is extremely clear that the president of the party, the president of the then-existing pretakeover Crisis Staff is Mr. Miskovic, and he, in fact, is the person who had dinner with Mr. Mujadzic, who did not have dinner with Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. The problem is only that unfortunately, the English translation we have before us starts at another portion. If we compare it with the B/C/S we have before us, in B/C/S, you can't read the first sentence how it all happened and the name before. It doesn't start with a name in B/C/S. And if you could please, additionally, give us a hint when was this tape taken? We know it's about 1803 or 1804 hours, but not the day when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if I would be able to tell Your Honours that. This was a tape that was seized. I think at one point -- I have to through this again, but I think at one point they indicate that this is the anniversary of the takeover several years later. A note on one of my documents indicates 1995, so it would be the April 29th or April 30th of 1995. But it's definitely clear from the context that it's talking about the takeover several years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's right. But of course, it would be of interest which year it indeed was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can tell you it was seized in 1997. So it was before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Somewhere between 1992 and 1997. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At one point, if you look on page 3728, the last four digits of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I mentioned this, it's 18.03 or 18.04.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What I'm looking at is on page 3728. It indicates from the reporter: "This is a good occasion to make a parallel at the end of our conversation and compare the SDS then in April 1992 and now in April 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this clarification. Having this background, we can continue, and let's hear the next portion until the end of the contribution of Mr. Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please stop. May we hear now the English and French version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Reporter: Dear listeners, this was Mr. Simo Drljaca who spoke in detail about the preparations and the seizure of power. I have to say right away that here, with us, are also Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Kuruzovic who are going to comment on these events from the point of view of the police and the former Serbian Army which was then called the TO staff of the Serbian Army. They are going to talk about how it looked from their perspective, since Mr. Simo Drljaca, Simo Miskovic said that the Crisis Staff concluded that it had to be done and acted accordingly. Music. Reporter: It is three or four minutes past 6.00, that is, if the clock is showing the correct time here in the Crvena Sala of the Express Restaurant of the Ljubija Ironworks. In this broadcast we remember April 1992, the time when on the night of the 29th, the decision was reached that the SDS, that is, the people from the SDS should take all the prominent positions and assume all the vital functions in the territory of Prijedor Municipality. One of the men who actually participated in all these decisions and activities taken on the night of the 29th was Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic, the former commander of the TO of the town of Prijedor who we would like to, first of all, welcome. Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic, this is the right moment to remember once again, after Mr. Simo Miskovic, the night of the 29th and also to stretch our memory a little bit further into the past and recall some of the times that had preceded these events. Slobodan Kuruzovic: As regards the political assessment of the situation, Simo and Dusan Kurnoga, the present -- the current president of the municipality have already covered it and said what had to be said. I would like to focus on the military aspect, and I would like to relate the situation chronologically, in a manner of speaking, and explain what happened and how it happened. Sometime around noon, this infamous Jerko Doko from Sarajevo sent this official dispatch, and we Serbs should perhaps be grateful to him because of that. Otherwise, we would have hesitated even more, which would have been extremely difficult to do since, as Dusan Kurnoga correctly pointed out, each and every one of us placed our families in jeopardy, since we had to do something which had never been done before, and that is to seize power. The situation was pretty clear, as explain as a pike staff, as our people say. It was clear what they were up to and what they were going to do to us. We knew exactly their location, how they were armed, where, and how they were trained in Kozarac, up there in Benkovac, Hambarine, and Puharska. We knew who had brought the weapons and how they were organised. We knew everything. It was in the air. As Simo said earlier, this Jerko Doko helped us by sending us this dispatch, and they thought that the Serbs would never get hold of that dispatch since the Muslims were in power. But they were wrong. Within 15 minutes, the dispatch was in my hands. I read it, and then we sat down and agreed on how we should proceed. As Simo said, at 5.00 p.m., we went up there to the barracks to discuss our military tactics and decide when and what was to be done. Dr. Stakic, former president of the municipality, myself, Drljaca, Jankovic, and Cadzo, Miskovic as the chairman of the SDS, and Lieutenant-Colonel Arsic were there. Arsic then held the rank of Lieutenant-Colonel and was the commander of the barracks and the commander of the 43rd Brigade. This group of people discussed this until nearly 7.00, and Arso insisted to decide that the moment was right and that it had to be done right away with no special preparations since we had had enough force at our disposal to prevent a massacre from occurring in the town. In that case, the consequences would have been unforeseeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now access to the original tape. And if there should be any problems as regards authenticity, the party may object. But in principle, I believe we can proceed now as follows: That we hear on one channel the tape in B/C/S, and on the other channel in English to be read out the text before us, and the French. I know very well it's not possible to do it simultaneously or not even parallelly, but it doesn't matter. It's just to give access to the content of this document in the three languages that are needed in this case. And let's try to proceed this way, if it's technically possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just a suggestion, perhaps the tape could be stopped after every approximately five minutes and the booth can wait for the interpreters to catch up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we should be aware that it's nearly impossible to catch up or to read or translate even parallelly. So no doubt, B/C/S will be finished first, then English, then French. But it doesn't matter. I can't see any other solution. Let's try it this way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Reporter, before the 29th and 30th of April 1992, Serbian people tried in every conceivable way to preserve peace, not only in the Municipality of Prijedor, but wider in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina by offering to the SDA various proposals for an agreement. What we are interested in here and what our listeners would like to hear is if you are depict the atmosphere in that room where you were making this important decision between let's say 1400 or 1500 and 1700 hours. Kuruzovic: It is difficult is to describe that. A moment ago, I wanted to say something in this respect. It was an uneasy situation to do something like this. It was obvious that we held no power, either in Prijedor or at the republican level. It was such a big town, and so many people who were not in harmony with us, and the political problems concerning the division of power and all other issues were dragging on for a year and a half, and the situation was very complicated. However, the decision was made, and we agreed, that the takeover should be carried out by the police, who together with the Croats and Muslims wore those blue uniforms, trying to maintain law and order in the town, and we decided that they should do it down here in the town whereas that the military aspect, which was under my authority, should be taken care by us. In other words, that this takeover should be secured by the armed Serbs. Allow me to put things in chronological perspective. After that agreement, sometime around 1900 hours, Captain Bojic, Captain Savic, myself and the late Major Karlica sat down and drew up a plan. We had everything in front of us, the whole town and the combat disposition of the forces. It is no secret any more. We knew exactly where they had their people and units. They even had arms, et cetera. At 2100 hours, of course, it was the 29th April, 1992, I summoned all commanders of the regional staffs in our town, both from urban and suburban areas, settlements, and villages. They came to that building of the Slovenian company in the field in Cirkin Polje, where later the HQ of the Serbian TO staff was established and whose commander I was. I had been officially appointed by the Serbian Municipal Assembly and we agreed on how to proceed and the mobilisation was ordered to be carried out at 0200 hours a.m. All armed Serbs in the settlements, suburban areas, and villages were supposed to take their positions at the given moment. We agreed on the manner how it should be done. They had to be ready to enter the town strictly upon my order at 4.00 a.m., if need be. And that's what happened. In the meantime, Simo, Dule Jankovic, Cadzo, and many others such as Marko Djenadija, Jakovljevic, Pop Mudrinic and others from the police, who need not to be mentioned now, but who had done a lot of work. This reserve police force came to the dom in Cirkin Polje. According to our assessment, the callups were sent out for 260 people for the job. However, a lot more appeared. That is partly an answer to the question. This hall was fully packed and people talked and smoked. No one made noise or shouted. I have no words to depict the atmosphere in that room. People were aware of the seriousness of the task ahead of us and they acted according to the situation. At 4.00, the first convoys, so to speak, of people who were organised and tasked to take over all vital buildings and functions in the municipality set off. This little mini-bus that Mico Janjetovic used to take the Rudar players to the soccer matches in was used and the rounds were made to the SUP, the Court, the municipal building, the Kozarski Vjesnik, et cetera. Maybe this might sound funny, but the last building that was taken was the Public Auditing Service, because the guard there who was a Serb had fallen asleep, and I vividly remember how we sat in that room, Simo, Djule Jankovic, Cadzo, and myself, listening to the man talking on the Motorola whether they should break in through the door or not, and someone said: "Why bother breaking in, since he would wake up eventually" and that's what happened. There were no incidents, nothing, and at 4.25, the last report came through. The procedure was rather simple. One would just say "over." And that was a sign that the task was completed, i.e., that a certain office i.e., function had been taken. And that was it. At 4.25, it was all over. At 5.00, the representatives of our Serbian authorities came to me to the HQ, the president of the municipality, the vice-president of the municipality, chairman of the executive committee, secretary for the economy, defence minister, and all the others, according to the respective departments in the municipality, and then we began dispatching them. There were also a few prominent general managers there. There's no need to name everyone. They went to their respective offices, where our armed policemen were waiting for them with the lists of the people who were not to be allowed to enter the municipal building, the Court, the SUP building, and so on, not those who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could. Simo has just mentioned that, and I think it is good idea that we luckily came to that smart idea that the president of the municipality, the chairman of the party, and some top officials, supporters of the SDA, were not granted access, while all other Muslims or Croats, regardless of nationality and regular employees came to work as usual, the only difference being that the Serbian flag and the Yugoslav flag were hoisted up on the municipal building to mark that the takeover had been carried out. By 6.00 a.m., it was all over. We informed Vojo Kupresanin in Banja Luka. At that time, there was still the Autonomous Region of the Krajina, since everything had not been done yet. He could not believe when we told him it was over and that we have seized the power in the municipality, since it was much more difficult to do it here than in those smaller towns like Novi Dubica, Sana, because, and it is well known, we were a big regional centre and the chief of this regional centre was this Mirza Mujadzic, and since Simo has already said everything about him, there is no need for me to repeat. Reporter: Since this action to seize power in the municipality had been meticulously planned and carried out without a single incident or shot being fired, we would like to know what were the assessments that afternoon on 29th. Did you expect an immediate reaction on the part of the SDA, and what would have been your course of action had something like that happened? Kuruzovic: It is very difficult to answer to the first part of the question with regard to their possible reaction. I do not know if the time is right to discuss all that, but we knew that they had been armed, we knew where they were, we knew where their strongest units were, but there was something else about which they did not pay attention all the while. As Simo said, As we were trying the democratic option and trying to draw to their attention to that was wrong and -- later throughout that month. Maybe it's not okay that I say that, as the general manager of our company, but we will talk about what happened during that month here in Prijedor. We fought in the western Slavonija for a year, and they did not, and that was our enormous advantage since we knew that they did not stand a ghost of a chance to do something so drastic. And eventually it proved right when 120 of them carried that attack thinking that they could do something using rifles, and you know how this attempt ended. Our assumption was -- we predicted that nothing silly would happen, in other words, that they might cause an incident, because in each and every Serbian village, in every part of the town of Prijedor, in every suburban settlement where the Serbs lived, everything was organised. Reporter: Were you much surprised by the action which ensued on 29 or 30 May when the Muslims, Muslim fanatics of the SDA attacked the town of Prijedor? Kuruzovic: We expected something like that any day, because we knew they could not get over that. Our people will proudly remember that, and their people will remember it as well, although they will judge it differently. We simply outsmarted them and seized power in 25 minutes without having fired a single shot, because we did not want it to happen any other way. Let me take the opportunity and remind you that even before that, there were many problems. There were burglaries, robberies et cetera, in the town, and that was one of the compelling reasons since we wanted to prevent that. They did not surprise us because we knew they did not have respectable force, but I was personally surprised a little bit because this Slavko Acimovic was my pupil. I could not believe it. He was something of an enigma. We knew he had been plotting something and that he was a member of the HDZ, but that he was capable of something like that, that was beyond expectation. I know why that happened. We talked a lot about that later on. They did not want that much to seize power. Their intention was to excuse themselves before their own people. Alija is doing something similar at the moment. He constantly attacks and reports casualties. Let me not mention all of it now, but for instance, the Markale incident, or the French being killed, et cetera, et cetera, merely to prove that something is being done. Maybe it is not fair to talk like this, but I know they took a hell of a lot of money from their people in order to procure weapons to attack the Serbs, slaughter them, and eventually cause an exodus. We struggled for a month to persuade them to disarm and hand in those weapons, to resolve all the problems, preserve peace and schedule elections - we don't care who wins - to preserve peace and order in the town, but to no avail. Of course, in that case, they would have to return the money to the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and listen until we have the end of the French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Reporter: This is a good occasion to make a parallel at the end of our conversation and to compare the SDS then in April 1992 and now in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The French version is also done?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French interpreters finished at the same time as the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's have a break of half an hour now, until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May we now continue in the way we did it. May we so start the B/C/S version, and then at the same time start with English and French. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] This is Prijedor radio, live broadcast from the Crvena sala of the express restaurant of the Ljubija mine ironworks and the studio of the Prijedor radio. And now we are going to play some music and let the colleagues from the studio take over. Reporter: And so dear listeners, we have slowly brought this programme to an end. Today we look back on the 30th of April, 1992, when the SDS assumed power in this town and this municipality. We heard a lot about immediate preparations, and the takeover. Our next guest, Mr. Mico Kovacevic, the first chairman of the executive committee of the Prijedor Municipality could tell us something about the functioning of the authorities. The SDS took power exactly at dawn on the 30th of April, and on the very same day, there was a session of our government which as Mico has said just now, as we are preparing this conversation, was a shadow government. Mr. Kovacevic, how do it all look back then? Kovacevic: I would first of all like to greet our listeners, if anyone is listening to us. I would not like to talk about the preparations since many before me commented on this, and on what it looked like. The question indicated that it did not altogether happen spontaneously, that it happened in a disorganised manner, et cetera. As those who preceded me already said in this programme, it is all very well prepared. Having seen that we did not stand a ghost of a chance in this Alija's unitarian state, I'm not interested in how he pictured that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please stop. The OTP has --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I'm correct, I just noticed on the English translation, I think because of some confusion when we ended, we actually lost about a page of the B/C/S. I think it stopped on page -- the translation at the break at page 3727, around the middle where it says Kuruzovic we simply outsmarted them and seized power because we did not want it to happen any other way. I think that was the end of the English translation, with this is Prijedor live broadcast. I'm mainly concerned about the French, and I didn't follow that. But I presume we might have lost the same or more on the French translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but I had the other impression that we had the break at the end of the contribution of Mr. Kuruzovic on page 33728. And then continuing...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I understand now, it's just the matter of the Live Note is behind, and the actual translation was done. So as long as the French booth and the English booth feel that they are up to date, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's difficult to see through the shaded glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I see the English says okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's continue where we just stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I'm concerned with how we pictured that. We did not deny anything to anyone, neither then nor now, but we have to pursue our right, and we will succeed one way or another. Serb must remain in a single state. Not in these Serbian Krajina, Krajina Serbia, Montenegro and whatnot. It's all the same to me. That's the course that we had taken then, and I believe the majority still adheres to the same principles. Otherwise, it would be no good. I would not like to make any further comments on the preparations. We had earlier formed the so-called shadow government. This is a political expression, although for us it was a government which had already been in function at the time. When we decided to do it, we did it the way we did it. We set up a staff. I'm not going to give any names. It is known. Someone knows. I do not have to know that. On today's date, we had talks about it, and scheduled the date and all that, and then we decided that we should do it on such and such a day at a certain hour. The government was there from the president of the municipality to those structures which I am still not familiar with, evening after two years in power, since it does not interest me. My field is medicine. Some were from the SDS, some from the executive committee. It was all neatly prepared and done, and we waited for that moment that we set, and then on today's date, at 4.00 a.m., a few years ago, we did what we did. To my own and everyone else's surprise, it really went the way we had planned it, I mean, those from the SUP, that is to say, from the centre, Simo and others, told me that they had announced from our HQ that the movement was to begin, and in 28 minutes, I was in the position of the chairman of the executive committee, and Stakic held the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly. All bodies of authority were in their positions and began functioning from that moment on. Therefore, some kind of transition was made from those national parties. Today, opinions may vary. But those were indeed national parties, and it is good that it was done the way it was done. So 20 minutes after setting out from Cirkin Polje, the municipality resumed its work as if nothing had happened. That was done without casualties or shooting. Nothing. We just came to our respective offices and began working, as if it had been for centuries like that. And thank God it still goes on like that. A lot has been sacrificed and a high price has been paid but it is all right as long as the price is not even higher. Reporter: When you took on the duty as the chairman of the first Executive Committee of the former Serbian Assembly, that is, Prijedor Municipality, in addition to the difficulties and problems that plagued you at the time, that plagued at the time, not only Prijedor but this entire region, you had yet another demanding task which you, from our point of view, fulfilled in a rather charming manner. You were the first man in Prijedor to receive foreign journalists and explain what was going on. How did you do that? Kovacevic: I followed a rather simple principle. As a doctor and a humanist by profession, I dealt with it accordingly. Up until then I treated people regardless of nationality, race, colour of skin. I do not know what the principle was well established in the field of medicine. It is not relevant whether a person is yellow, white, Muslim, Catholic, Buddhist or Orthodox by faith. It was all the same to me. However, journalists approached me with provocative questions, and I simply followed the principle to which I still adhere today. Even today, I could successfully deal with any delegation from CNN to ICRC. You can verify this in Banja Luka. For example, I just received a new representative. My principle was the truth. I present them with the bare and unpleasant truth, and I disarmed them on the spot. I placed my cards on the table equally for those from CNN and those from Russia who usually lack information just like you and for all the others, regardless of their confession. I played poker with all the cards on the table. I used to play it, and now I'm an elderly man and I have other responsibilities. And then we play, and he cannot fool me over anything. It was the easiest thing for me. If you use the trigger, too, I knew them immediately, but I did not want to use them on purpose, and he had to succumb. Sometimes I had the courage to say things. I'm not afraid of any one of those 21 cells in The Hague. I then said: "Take me and Genscher before the court and then we'll see who is going to be hanged on this Cyrillic letter G. They gave me a firm promise that they would translate it like that both for the CNN and in Germany, but they did now. I got the information. I know that he was not playing a fair game with me. As soon as you are hiding something, you are handicapped. I can easily deal with this type. That was my principle. Reporter: Dear listeners, that is our interlocutor earned the nickname "Pukovnik," Colonel, although he is not one. All foreign journalists called him Pukovnik just because of his outspoken attitude, his eloquence, and the agility with which he presented the truth. Thank you for the participation in this conversation. Kovacevic: I would like to insert a correction. Reporter: Please. Kovacevic: I told everyone and those who listened to me understood. They do not want to listen. They come with their own truth. I told everyone I am a colonel in the medical corps who was retired at his own expense. Often they do not know how to translate that and they do not know what they are searching for. No one can promote or demote me, or strip me of my rank. Best regards to the listeners. Reporter: We thank "the colonel who was retired at this own expense." Excerpts from the session of the Municipal Assembly broadcast by Prijedor Radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, it's right for the parties to give observations on this issue, on the tape we just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could ask, I don't know if the translation stopped before the end of the announcement. I think there's some significance to that, because it's talking about the consequences of not accepting the Vance-Owen plan. It's just an additional way of placing the tape in a time sequence, that it was 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But is it related to the reporter, and I think the reporter closed "retired at his own expense" and then there is a new -- it seems to be only headlines. And I can't see the relevance of this additional part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I could be wrong. My understanding is this is just a continuation of the same tape, may be a new segment starting. But Your Honour just asked me about the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you please compare the last page in B/C/S, you can see that it ends with "we thank the Colonel who is retired at his own expense." And the following, you can't find in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I see it wasn't put on the transcript, but it's on the tape. If Your Honours don't think it's helpful, that's fine with me. Just you asked about the time; I think it helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently one couldn't find it on the same side of the tape, and as it reads in English, side B seems to be empty. But please, it's the right of the parties to comment on that what we have heard. Any observations by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we could follow regarding the translation, it was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And as -- of course, we can't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course you can't cross-examine, but it's your right to comment also on the content of these parts we just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we object to the authenticity, Your Honour, of this tape, because we just heard that it has been seized, but we don't know where. Maybe Mr. Inayat can help when he comes. But for now, we would like to reserve our right to object to this tape as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Inayat will testify that it was seized in December 1997 from the Prijedor radio station. But I think the tape --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's good to know that it's contested, whenever we have a new witness from the area, knowing the acting persons there, we can once again play and ask whether or not a person can identify the voice of these persons we heard on the tape. We shouldn't forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No other comments. Then nevertheless, under the rules, we had until now, and we continue without doubt with these rules. This is admitted into evidence under the number given before, -1. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, we would like to -- we would like the Chamber to instruct the OTP not to play this tape to the witnesses prior to their testimony. The other way they could be instructed who is who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't hope that any party instructs a witness to give a certain testimony, but indeed, it could be preferable to hear the tape in the courtroom, and then ask the witness whether or not the voice can be identified. But then let's proceed. We heard in the beginning of this session that the OTP is prepared to tender another set of documents. And is it the understanding, this would be now List 5? Do you agree to have it as List 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And we -- the actual list is on top of the documents. If I could just make one brief comment regarding the last matter raised by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, don't hesitate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has imposed some time limitations on our case. We're trying to focus our case on real issues. There's -- this is a tape that was seized from the radio station in Prijedor. I don't think a court of law we should lose basic common sense. There's absolutely no evidence right now that the people named in that tape a Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Kovacevic, Mr. Kuruzovic, are not the people that were speaking. It really doesn't -- common sense tells you that those were the people that were speaking. I don't think the OTP intends to waste time, given the reasonable limits that the Court has imposed on us on things that are not in issue. We don't see an issue. If the Defence raises one, we can address it. But this is just common sense that these are the people that are speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have heard the message, and no doubt there is a lot of truth in this message. Let's turn to the documents immediately. Could the OTP please be so kind and give us some guidance when we are going through these documents now. And let's do it in the way that you indicate which document is of special importance from your point of view in order that it can be read out. On the other hand, it should be the -- first of all, on the question of whether or not to admit into evidence these documents. Please, feel free to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I selected these documents. I think all are very relevant, but there may be in some of the longer documents, there may be only portions that are relevant. And if that's the case, I will indicate to the Court. Also, some of these we only have draft translations, on just a few of these. But the first one is 65 ter number 5 involves a certificate on the election to the post of Municipal Assemblyman. I would ask that be marked next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please have the next exhibit number. 190. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I see, unfortunately, on this one, we have both a translation and a draft. Never mind. Apparently you don't have that. You have the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the registry, please, the next following number is 190. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I look at this exhibit list. The next number should be S189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't we have that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the diagram of the courtroom that we marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. So 65 ter number 5 then receives S190. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I have these documents with me. Can we go with the possible objections afterwards when I discuss these documents with Dr. Stakic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Then we proceed this way, that we give a provisional exhibit number, as we did it in the past, for the documents and decide later on on the admission. Therefore, this is now S190. And may S190 provisional be read out in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Form number 21, [Article 19, item 6, and Article 22, item 4] of the law. "Municipal electoral committee Prijedor. "01-193/90. "Prijedor, 11 December, 1990. "Signed, president Nedzad Seric. Secretary, Radmila Majkic".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one where we have a draft translation. It was 65 ter number 8. This would be now provisional S191, A and B respectively. Has document such an importance that it's necessary to be read out?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Socialist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just a minute. The OTP may --

utterances.text: I don't have an objection to reading it all out, but if I can just indicate --

utterances.text: Yes. I can indicate that in this report of the election commission, it indicates which people were elected from various parts of the municipality. utterances.text: I believe it's not necessary to read out this entire document. We can see on page 7 that in the Omarska electoral district, assemblyman of the Serbian democratic party is Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.text: Yes. And there are several names that have come up in the testimony such as that -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. another person elected from the reformist party was Riza Beglerbegovic.

utterances.text: It's twice the same document, I believe. The document in B/C/S that has the ERN range of 00633787 to 3788 was seized from a police station, while the following document with the range P0007162 to 7163 was seized from the Municipal Assembly building. Again, since the authenticity of the documents are at issue, the fact that the document was found twice at two different locations, we think it's relevant that both be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then not yet admitted, but provisionally, the one starting with -- ending with S787 will be now 192B-1. And the other one ending with the number 7162 will be 192B-2. May we now, please, hear the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Article of the constitutional act on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina stipulate that the laws and other regulations of the SFRJ were applied until such time as the appropriate laws and other regulations of the republic are passed, provide that they conform to the constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, do we have the same document before us? It should read 00916642.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first page is missing from my document here. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I help you out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Article 12 of the constitutional act on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina [Official gazette of the Serbian people in BH, number 3/92] Article 46 of the law of basic property and legal relations [Official gazette of the Socialist federal Republic of Yugoslavia, number 6/80], the decision of the assembly and the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, number 03-300/92, dated 28 April; and 03-513/92, dated 19 June, 1992; and Article 230 of the statute of the Prijedor Municipality [Official gazette of the Prijedor Municipality number 7/84, 9/85, 1/90, 6/90, and 1/91] the Prijedor Municipal Assembly passed the following decision at its session held on 1992, passed the following decision on proclaiming abandoned property, property of the state: Paragraph "Article 1: All abandoned property [Real estate and moveable items] of persons who have left the territory of the Prijedor Municipality, and of persons who participated in the armed uprising, is temporarily proclaimed state property, the Prijedor Municipality becoming entitled to all possession rights. "Article 2: The municipal secretariat for city planning, housing, and utilities, and legal property affairs, and the municipal land survey department, in cooperation with other municipal organs, shall make an inventory of all real estate [Land, family houses, business premises, property and economic facilities] belonging to persons referred to in Article 1 of this decision. Article 3: The allotment of the property referred to in Article 1 of this decision will be determined by a separate decision of the Municipal Assembly. "Article 4: This decision shall be effective until the appropriate legislation for these matters has been passed by the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Article 5: This decision comes into effect on the day on which it is passed and will be published in the official gazette of the Prijedor Municipality. "Signed, president of the municipal assembly, Dr. Milomir Stakic. "Rationale, legal grounds: "Article 12 of the constitutional act on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and decision of the Assembly on the Autonomous Region of Krajina stipulate that the laws and other regulations of the SFRJ will apply until such time as the appropriate laws and other regulations of the Republic are passed, provided that they con form to the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the laws and other regulations passed by the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the People's Assembly. Therefore, the legal grounds for this decision are found in Article 46 of the federal law on basic property and legal rights which stipulates that the right of ownership terminates with abandonment and that abandoned real estate becomes socially owned property at the time it was abandoned. "In addition to the above-mentioned legal grounds, additional legal ground can be found in the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, which stipulates that all the abandoned property must immediately be registered and then declared state property, with the municipality claiming full ownership rights. "Reasons for reaching this decision: A certain number of people have left the municipality and abandoned their property. There is also property that belongs to those who participated in the armed uprising and their property should temporarily be declared state property so that it can be allocated for use. The proclamation for state property is temporary because appropriate legal regulations will be passed in relation to this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I just inquire of the Trial Chamber, some of the other documents that had even an typed signature, I know the documents with the actual handwritten signature, Your Honour wanted the originals. I don't know if you want to have the originals of the typed signatures only but if so, we can provide that. When I say the originals, I mean the document we have in evidence, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. We have to be aware that no doubt -- no date is filled in, both in the beginning and at the end of the document. And even the line that reads "number" is not filled in. So probably, maybe it's only a draft. We have to come back to this later when we have an overview of all the documents. The same is true, and I think because it's in close connection so that what we just recently heard, and it's open to the parties to read themselves, the next document needs not to be read out, but of course we attribute a provisional number, and this would be for 65 ter Document Number 45, it should be S193, A and B respectively. Then we may turn to 65 ter number 48. It's the same. It's not dated. And no number has been attributed, but nevertheless, following the policy, it may turn out, I don't know, that some of these documents appear in the official gazette then later on. The former 48 will now be provisional S194, A and B respectively, hoping that this time, you have both pages. Could you please read out the English document. 48, now 194.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Article 12 of the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina [Official gazette of the Serbian people in BH number 3/82] Article 5, paragraph 1, and Article 34 of the law on housing [Official gazette of the SR/Serbian Republic of BiH, number 14/84 and 12/87] And Article 230 of the statute of the Municipality of Prijedor number 7/84, 9/85, 6/90, and 2/91], the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor at its session on 1992 adopted the following decision on amendments to the decision on the conditions and mode of allocation for use of apartments at the disposal of the Municipality of Prijedor. "Article 1: In the decision on the conditions and mode of allocation for use of apartments at the disposal of the Municipality of Prijedor [Official Gazette of the Municipality of Prijedor number 5/85 and 4/91] in Article 14, after paragraph 1, new paragraphs 2 and 3 are added which read as follows: `Apartments from paragraph 1 of this article, once they are emptied of people and belongings, shall be registered in the housing fund for soldiers of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. `The Centre for Social Welfare shall immediately inform the competent organ and enable the use of these apartments.' "Article 2: The professional service is authorised to finalise the redacted text of the decision. "Article 3: This decision shall come into effect on the date of its adoption and will be published in the Official Gazette of the Municipality of Prijedor. "President of the Municipal Assembly, Dr. Milomir Stakic. "Statement of reasons, Article 1 and paragraph 4, and Article 14, paragraph 1 of the decision on the conditions and means of allocation for use of the apartments at the disposal of the Municipality of Prijedor prescribe that apartments obtained by the Municipality on the grounds of nationalisation and confiscation shall be given for use solely to persons who are in a situation of social need, on the basis of the recommendations of the Centre for Social Welfare in Prijedor. "Due to the pronounced need for a large number of apartments and their allocation to the participants in the war, it is necessary to register these apartments with the housing fund for soldiers of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. "Since substantial amendments were made to the decision in 1991, a redaction of the text is necessary, for which the SO professional service has been authorised."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And now for document former 65 ter 49, it will have provisionally the number S195A and B respectively. As to the fact that the content is closely related to the document we just heard, I think it's not necessary to read out this document. The following one, the former 65 ter 55 [Realtime transcript read in error "95"] would now provisionally have the number S196A and B respectively. Here, it's a total issue, and therefore I would ask the registry to read out this document in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "Pursuant to Articles 3 and 7 of the decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality, at a session held on, the war presidency of the Prijedor Municipality adopted a decision: "Article 1: This decision establishes the criteria for the division of real estate declared to be state or municipal property, residential buildings, family homes [Hereinafter referred to as property] among the Serbian population of Prijedor Municipality, families of fallen combatants, and the Serbian population moving in from areas affected by the war [Hereinafter refugees]. "Article 2: Citizens have the right to a share in this property according to the following categories: "1, the first category applies to citizens of Serbian nationality who have been left without property as a result of the fighting in Prijedor Municipality. "2, the second category applies to citizens left without property who have refugee status and wish to reside permanently in Prijedor Municipality. "The third category applies to combatants of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who have no property or whose property is insufficient for future existence. "Article 3: When resolving the division of property, the relevant administrative organs will take into account the status of property of citizens, meaning the size and value of property lost and destroyed, and that the property apportioned be of approximately the same size and value of the property lost or destroyed. "Members of the military and families of fallen combatants shall have priority in the right established in the preceding paragraph within the group to which they belong according to the criteria established above.
